subject: science
name: Temperature and its Measurement
summary: Touch cannot tell us exactly how hot or cold something is, so we measure temperature with a thermometer. This chapter covers what temperature is, the Celsius scale, clinical and digital thermometers for body temperature, laboratory thermometers for other things, how to read a thermometer correctly and safely, and how air temperature is measured for weather reports.

topics.title: Hot or cold? Why touch can fool us
topics.summary: Our sense of touch can tell hot from cold roughly, but it is not reliable for knowing exactly how hot something is.
topics.simple: We can feel that a cup of tea is hot and an ice cube is cold. But our hands can be fooled. If one hand has been in cold water and the other in warm water, the same lukewarm water feels warm to one hand and cool to the other! So we need a tool to tell us exactly how hot or cold something is.
topics.explain:
In daily life we use words like **hot**, **warm**, **cool** and **cold**. Water from a tap feels warm on a summer afternoon, while water from the fridge feels cold. Some things are clearly hotter than others.

But **touch is not reliable**. Try this activity:
1. Take three bowls: one with cold water, one with lukewarm (slightly warm) water, and one with warm water that is comfortable to touch (never hot!).
2. Dip your left hand in the cold water and your right hand in the warm water for a minute.
3. Now put both hands in the lukewarm water.

The left hand feels the lukewarm water as **warm**, while the right hand feels it as **cool**. The water is the same, but your hands disagree!

Touch also has other problems:
- We cannot touch very hot things (like boiling water or a hot iron) without getting hurt.
- Touch cannot give a number, so we cannot compare exactly.
- When a mother touches a child's forehead to check for fever, she can only guess. A doctor needs an exact value.

That is why we need a **reliable measure** of hotness or coldness. This measure is called **temperature**, and the instrument used to measure it is a **thermometer**.
topics.example: In winter, a steel chair and a wooden chair in the same room are at the same temperature, but the steel one feels much colder to touch. Our skin is not a good judge of temperature!
keyPoints: Touch can only roughly tell hot from cold
The same water can feel warm to one hand and cool to the other
We cannot safely touch very hot objects
Touch gives no exact number to compare
We need a thermometer for a reliable measurement

topics.title: Temperature and the Celsius scale
topics.summary: Temperature is a reliable measure of how hot or cold something is; in India we usually measure it in degrees Celsius (°C).
topics.simple: **Temperature** tells us how hot or cold something is, as a number. A higher temperature means hotter. We usually write temperature in **degrees Celsius**, like 37 °C. Ice melts at 0 °C and water boils at 100 °C.
topics.explain:
**Temperature** is a reliable measure of the hotness or coldness of an object. The hotter an object, the higher its temperature. If object A has a higher temperature than object B, then A is hotter than B.

Temperature is measured with a **thermometer**.

**The Celsius scale**
The scale we use most in India is the **Celsius scale**. Its unit is the **degree Celsius**, written as **°C**. So 25 degrees Celsius is written as 25 °C.

Two useful fixed points on this scale:
- Ice melts (and pure water freezes) at **0 °C**
- Pure water boils at **100 °C** (at normal air pressure)

The gap between 0 °C and 100 °C is divided into 100 equal parts, and each part is 1 degree.

**Other scales**
- The **Fahrenheit scale** (°F) is still used for body temperature in some places. Normal body temperature is about **98.6 °F**, which is the same as about 37 °C.
- Scientists use the **kelvin** (K), which is the SI unit of temperature. You will learn more about it in higher classes.

**Temperatures below zero**
Some places get colder than 0 °C. These temperatures are written with a minus sign, for example −5 °C (read as 'minus five degrees Celsius'). Places like Leh and Dras in Ladakh go far below 0 °C in winter.
topics.deep: If you are curious: you can change Celsius into Fahrenheit using F = (9/5 × C) + 32. For example, 37 °C → (9/5 × 37) + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = 98.6 °F. You do not need to memorise this in Class 6.
topics.example: A weather report says Delhi was 45 °C in May and 5 °C in January. You can tell straight away that May was much hotter, because 45 is much higher than 5.
keyPoints: Temperature = reliable measure of hotness or coldness
Higher temperature means hotter
Measured with a thermometer
Common unit: degree Celsius (°C)
Ice melts at 0 °C; water boils at 100 °C
Normal body temperature ≈ 37 °C ≈ 98.6 °F
SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K)

topics.title: Measuring body temperature: clinical and digital thermometers
topics.summary: A clinical thermometer measures human body temperature; its range is about 35 °C to 42 °C, and safer digital thermometers are now replacing mercury ones.
topics.simple: To check if someone has fever, we use a **clinical thermometer**. It only reads from about 35 °C to 42 °C, because a person's body temperature stays in this range. Today most families use a **digital thermometer**, which shows the number on a small screen and beeps when ready.
topics.explain:
A **clinical thermometer** is made specially to measure the temperature of the **human body**.

**Range:** about **35 °C to 42 °C**. Our body temperature normally never goes outside this range, so a wider scale is not needed.

**Normal body temperature** is about **37 °C** (98.6 °F). It can be a little different for different people and at different times of the day, so a reading like 36.8 °C is also normal. A temperature clearly above normal means **fever**.

**Mercury clinical thermometers**
Older clinical thermometers have a thin glass tube with shiny **mercury** inside. They have a small bend called a **kink** near the bulb. The kink stops the mercury from falling back on its own, so you can read the temperature after taking it out of the mouth. Before using it again, it must be given a few jerks to bring the mercury below 35 °C.

Mercury is **poisonous**. If the thermometer breaks, mercury can harm people and the environment. So mercury thermometers are being replaced.

**Digital thermometers**
- Show the temperature as numbers on a screen, so they are easy to read
- Usually beep when the reading is ready
- Do not contain mercury, so they are safer

During the COVID-19 pandemic, you may have seen **non-contact (infrared) thermometers** pointed at people's foreheads at shop and school entrances.

**Using a clinical thermometer safely**
1. Wash it with soap and water (or an antiseptic) before and after use.
2. For a mercury thermometer, shake it so the level is below 35 °C.
3. Place the bulb under the tongue (or in the armpit) and wait about one minute, or until a digital one beeps.
4. Read the temperature, holding it by the end, not the bulb.
5. Never use a clinical thermometer to check hot water or anything else; it can break.
topics.example: Riya feels unwell. Her father uses a digital thermometer under her tongue and it beeps showing 38.5 °C. That is above normal (about 37 °C), so Riya has a fever and should see a doctor.
keyPoints: Clinical thermometer measures human body temperature
Range about 35 °C to 42 °C
Normal body temperature about 37 °C (98.6 °F)
Mercury thermometers have a kink to stop mercury falling back
Mercury is poisonous, so digital thermometers are preferred
Wash before and after use; never use it for hot water

topics.title: Laboratory thermometer and reading a thermometer correctly
topics.summary: A laboratory thermometer measures temperatures of things other than the body, usually from −10 °C to 110 °C, and must be held and read correctly.
topics.simple: To measure the temperature of water, milk or other things, we use a **laboratory thermometer**. It can read from about −10 °C to 110 °C. We must keep it straight, keep the bulb inside the liquid without touching the container, and read it with our eye at the level of the liquid inside.
topics.explain:
A **laboratory thermometer** is used to measure the temperature of objects other than the human body, such as water, oil or air, in experiments.

**Range:** usually **−10 °C to 110 °C**. It has **no kink**, so the liquid starts to fall as soon as you take it out. That is why you must read it **while the bulb is still in the substance**.

It contains a liquid that expands when heated: **mercury** (silvery) or **coloured alcohol** (often red).

**Finding the value of one small division**
1. Pick two marked numbers, e.g. 20 °C and 30 °C. Difference = 10 °C.
2. Count the small divisions between them, e.g. 10.
3. One division = 10 °C ÷ 10 = **1 °C**.

If there were 5 divisions between 20 and 30, each would be 10 ÷ 5 = 2 °C.

**Precautions while using it**
- Hold it **upright (vertical)**, not tilted.
- Keep the **bulb fully inside** the substance.
- The bulb must **not touch the bottom or sides** of the container.
- Wait until the liquid level stops moving.
- Read with your **eye level with the top of the liquid** column, not from above or below.
- Handle it gently; glass breaks easily.
- Do not use a laboratory thermometer to take body temperature, and do not use a clinical one for hot water.
topics.example: Aman measures the temperature of tap water. He holds the thermometer upright, keeps the bulb in the water away from the bottom of the glass, waits for the red line to stop, and reads 28 °C with his eye level with the top of the red line.
keyPoints: Used for things other than the human body
Range usually −10 °C to 110 °C
No kink, so read while bulb is in the substance
Contains mercury or coloured alcohol
One division = difference between marks ÷ number of divisions
Hold upright; bulb must not touch the container
Read with eye level with the liquid top

topics.title: Air temperature and weather reports
topics.summary: The temperature of the air changes during the day and across seasons; weather reports give the day's maximum and minimum temperatures.
topics.simple: The air around us has a temperature too. It is usually lowest early in the morning and highest in the afternoon. Weather reports on TV and in newspapers tell us the highest (**maximum**) and lowest (**minimum**) temperature of the day.
topics.explain:
Just like water or our body, the **air** has a temperature. Air temperature changes:
- **During the day:** it is usually lowest around early morning (just before sunrise) and highest in the early afternoon, after the Sun has heated the ground for hours.
- **Across seasons:** it is much higher in summer than in winter.
- **From place to place:** a hill station like Shimla is cooler than Chennai on the same day.

**Weather reports** in newspapers, on TV and on phone apps give the **maximum temperature** (highest that day) and **minimum temperature** (lowest that day) for different cities. These readings are taken by weather offices using special thermometers kept in the shade, so that sunlight falling directly on the thermometer does not give a wrong reading.

You can measure air temperature yourself with a laboratory thermometer: hang it in the shade, wait a few minutes, and note the reading at different times of the day. You will see a pattern.

Knowing air temperature helps farmers plan crops, helps people prepare for **heatwaves** and **cold waves**, and helps us choose what clothes to wear.
topics.example: A newspaper shows 'Jaipur: Max 41 °C, Min 27 °C'. The difference between the hottest and coolest time of that day was 41 − 27 = 14 °C.
keyPoints: Air also has a temperature
Usually lowest early morning, highest early afternoon
Higher in summer, lower in winter
Weather reports give daily maximum and minimum temperatures
Air temperature is measured in the shade
Useful for farmers and for heatwave or cold wave warnings

faqs.q: What is the difference between a clinical thermometer and a laboratory thermometer?
faqs.a:
- **Use:** clinical measures human body temperature; laboratory measures other things like water or air.
- **Range:** clinical about 35 °C to 42 °C; laboratory usually −10 °C to 110 °C.
- **Kink:** a mercury clinical thermometer has a kink so the reading stays; a laboratory thermometer has no kink, so you must read it while it is still in the substance.
keywords: difference between clinical and laboratory thermometer

faqs.q: Why can't we use a clinical thermometer to measure the temperature of boiling water?
faqs.a: A clinical thermometer only reads up to about 42 °C, because the human body never gets hotter than that. Boiling water is at 100 °C, far above its range. The liquid would expand too much and the thermometer could break.

faqs.q: Why are digital thermometers replacing mercury thermometers?
faqs.a: Mercury is poisonous. If a mercury thermometer breaks, the mercury can harm people and pollute the environment. Digital thermometers have no mercury, show the reading clearly as numbers and beep when ready, so they are safer and easier to use.

faqs.q: Is 37 °C the exact body temperature of every person?
faqs.a: No. About 37 °C (98.6 °F) is the *average* normal body temperature. It can be slightly lower or higher for different people, and it changes a little during the day. A reading like 36.7 °C is still normal. A reading clearly above normal means fever.

faqs.q: How do I find what one small division on a thermometer stands for?
faqs.a: Take two numbered marks, find their difference, and divide by the number of small divisions between them. Example: between 30 °C and 40 °C there are 10 divisions, so one division = (40 − 30) ÷ 10 = 1 °C.

quiz.q: Which of these is the most reliable way to know how hot a glass of water is?
quiz.explain: Touch can be fooled and the other senses don't give a number. A thermometer gives a reliable measurement.

quiz.q: One hand is kept in cold water and the other in warm water. Then both are put in lukewarm water. What happens?
options: Both hands feel it as hot
The hand from cold water feels it warm; the hand from warm water feels it cool
Both hands feel it as cold
quiz.explain: The same lukewarm water feels different to each hand. This shows touch is not reliable for judging temperature.

quiz.q: What is the normal temperature of the human body?
quiz.explain: Normal human body temperature is about 37 °C, which is 98.6 °F.

quiz.q: What is the usual range of a clinical thermometer?
quiz.explain: Human body temperature stays within about 35 °C to 42 °C, so a clinical thermometer only needs this range.

quiz.q: Why does a mercury clinical thermometer have a kink near its bulb?
options: To stop the mercury from falling back on its own
To make the mercury rise faster
quiz.explain: The kink holds the mercury in place after the thermometer is taken out, so the reading can be noted.

quiz.q: Which thermometer should be used to measure the temperature of hot tea?
options: Any clinical thermometer after shaking it
quiz.explain: Hot tea can be well above 42 °C, the upper limit of a clinical thermometer. A laboratory thermometer (up to about 110 °C) is the right choice.

quiz.q: On a thermometer, there are 5 small divisions between 20 °C and 30 °C. What does one division stand for?
Which of these is a WRONG way to use a laboratory thermometer?
options: Keeping the bulb fully in the liquid
Letting the bulb rest on the bottom of the beaker
Reading with the eye level with the liquid top
quiz.explain: The bulb must not touch the bottom or sides of the container, because the container may be hotter or colder than the liquid.

quiz.q: At what temperature does pure water boil (at normal air pressure)?
quiz.explain: On the Celsius scale, ice melts at 0 °C and pure water boils at 100 °C.

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of temperature?
quiz.explain: The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of temperature. In daily life in India we commonly use degree Celsius.

quiz.q: A weather report says: Max 39 °C, Min 26 °C. By how much did the temperature vary that day?
Why are digital thermometers considered safer than mercury thermometers?
quiz.explain: Mercury is poisonous and is dangerous if a thermometer breaks. Digital thermometers don't contain mercury.
